implementation_notes: Go's standard library replaces the route half of the structure with two calls - http.HandleFunc("/healthz", handler) registered on a ServeMux and served by http.ListenAndServe/http.Server - so what is left is the check set as ordinary functions returning an error or a status token and the status code written to the ResponseWriter (the Kubernetes documentation's own Go sample serves /healthz exactly this way, and controller-run time's healthz package is the framework-grade equivalent once a manager owns the process). The classic registry is still justified once checks need aggregation: keep them behind a struct, give each one a context with a deadline and cache the aggregate for the probe interval, otherwise a slow dependency makes the probe slower than the traffic it guards.
pitfalls: A check that calls a dependency without a context deadline lets the probe hang until the orchestrator's own timeout closes the connection, which is indistinguishable from an unreachable instance.

Serving health from the same http.Server as traffic makes a saturated server report unhealthy - sometimes intentional, but it must be a decision: a separate listener or a pre-warmed connection pool is the alternative.
A readiness handler that mutates state (starts a migration, warms a cache, opens a transaction) turns a harmless background poll into a repeated side effect; keep checks read-only.
